title: Can AI Chatbots Provide Coaching in Engineering? Beyond Information Processing Toward Mastery
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI chatbots can function as coaching tools in engineering education, with a particular focus on the boundary between technical support and deeper developmental guidance. The authors argue that engineering education is being reshaped by two simultaneous trends: the erosion of traditional apprenticeship-style mentoring and the rapid uptake of generative AI as an informal support tool. The central research questions ask how students and faculty perceive AI chatbots' role across technical, reflective, interpersonal, and ethical coaching domains, and what conditions around privacy, accountability, and transparency are required for acceptable use.

The empirical component is a mixed-methods perception study using surveys and brief open-ended responses. The study involved 75 engineering students and 7 engineering faculty members from Information Technology University in Pakistan. Survey items measured perceived usefulness across task domains, trust and relational boundaries, risk perception, and institutional safeguards. The study did not test a deployed chatbot intervention on learning outcomes; instead, it investigated stakeholder attitudes toward AI coaching before formal institutional integration. Quantitative analyses included descriptive statistics, composite scales, reliability analysis, and Welch's t-tests, while qualitative responses were thematically summarized.

Findings show conditional acceptance of AI coaching. Both students and faculty rated AI similarly useful overall for convergent tasks such as technical problem solving, concept clarification, and structured post-failure reflection. However, faculty perceived significantly greater risks than students, especially around over-trust, de-skilling, privacy, and inappropriate use in emotionally or ethically sensitive situations. Participants drew a strong boundary between acceptable AI uses for procedural and cognitive support versus unacceptable use for moral judgment, emotional support, and conflict management. Both groups strongly preferred AI as a supplement to, not a replacement for, human mentorship.

The paper concludes that generative AI can scale access to certain forms of engineering support, but it cannot replicate the embodied, relational, and value-laden dimensions of human coaching. The authors propose a multiplex coaching framework in which AI handles convergent, well-structured support tasks while human mentors remain responsible for divergent developmental work involving empathy, ethics, and contextual judgment. They also emphasize privacy-first governance, transparency, faculty preparation, and expert-in-the-loop design as prerequisites for responsible adoption.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbots used as coaching or support systems for learners, without a single specific product being the evaluated intervention.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an AI coaching chatbot in engineering education to assess student and faculty perceptions of its usefulness, risks, privacy requirements, and appropriate boundaries across convergent technical tasks versus divergent emotional/ethical/interpersonal tasks.

findings.finding_summary: In a mixed-methods perception study, students and faculty rated the perceived utility of AI coaching similarly for technical/academic support tasks: students M=3.84 (SD=0.62) and faculty M=3.83 (SD=0.58), with no significant between-group difference, t(9.85)=0.02, p=0.985, Cohen’s d=0.02. Item-level results indicated higher acceptance for convergent tasks such as getting unstuck on technical problems and concept clarification (both reported as M>4.0), with lower trust for divergent tasks such as team conflict management (students M=3.10, SD=1.08).
findings.measure: Perceived utility/usefulness of AI coaching across task domains on 5-point Likert scales; composite utility and item-level ratings

findings.finding_summary: Participants expressed strong skepticism about AI chatbots for emotional, moral, and contextual coaching. Faculty showed 0% trust in AI for emotional support roles, and students also preferred human mentors even when AI was available (reported as M>4.0 on mentor preference items), indicating AI was not accepted as a substitute for human support in affective and judgment-laden domains.
findings.measure: Trust/acceptance for emotional support, moral guidance, and human mentor preference on 5-point Likert items plus qualitative responses

findings.finding_summary: Faculty perceived significantly greater risk from AI coaching than students: faculty M=4.71 (SD=0.28) versus students M=4.14 (SD=0.54), t(7.65)=-3.98, p=0.003, Cohen’s d=1.34. This large effect suggests substantial concern among faculty about over-trust, privacy, and broader harms even though perceived utility was similar across groups.
findings.measure: Composite perceived risk on 5-point Likert scales

findings.finding_summary: Privacy emerged as a key deployment condition for AI coaching systems: 64.6% of students and 71.4% of faculty said conversation logs must remain completely private and inaccessible to instructors. Additional privacy governance preferences included anonymized data being acceptable for 29.2% of students and 42.9% of faculty, while only 16.7% of students and 28.6% of faculty supported full instructor access.
findings.measure: Privacy and data governance preferences from survey frequency distributions

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods perception study from a single institution with convenience samples (75 students, 7 faculty). It reports descriptive and inferential statistics, but it does not test causal effects on learning outcomes or coaching effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a large group difference in perceived risk (d=1.34), but outcomes are attitudes and acceptance rather than demonstrated student learning gains. Overall educational impact remains unclear because no causal achievement or behavior effects were measured.
